evidence_passages.passage: Repository metadata describes the article as an assessment of the effectiveness of an ozone foam fractionation system for PFAS removal from landfill leachate and quantification of equilibrium PFAS adsorption at the gas–water interface, with comparison to air foam fractionation.

source_limitations: This record duplicates the primary article already represented in WEB30; it is included only as repository confirmation and does not add new quantitative results.
No additional details on operating time, energy use or foamate management are provided beyond what appears in the main article.
source.title: PFAS removal from landfill leachate by ozone foam fractionation: System optimization and adsorption quantification (repository metadata)

sources.citation: Smith SJ, Wiberg K, McCleaf P, Ahrens L. ACS ES&T Water. 2022;2:841–851.

evidence_chunks.text: "The present study investigated the applicability of a pilot-scale foam fractionation setup for the removal of PFAS from natural landfill leachate in a novel continuous operating mode. A benchmark batch test was also performed to compare treatment efficiency."

The sum PFAS removal efficiency plateaued at about 60% in the continuous pilot column, while individual long-chain PFAS achieved removals above 90% and select short-chain PFAS showed low removals below roughly 30%.

"Differences in treatment efficiency between enriching mode versus stripping mode as well as between continuous versus batch mode were negligible. Taken together, these findings suggest that continuous foam fractionation is a highly applicable treatment technology for PFAS contaminated water."

The authors state that coupling this cost- and energy‑efficient foam fractionation pretreatment to an energy‑intensive degradative technology for the concentrated foam would be a promising strategy for on‑site PFAS remediation.

Enhanced foam collection (e.g., vacuum‑assisted collection) and combining several foam fractionation steps in series are suggested as options to improve short‑chain PFAS removal and overall performance.

source_limitations: Study focuses on a single landfill leachate; PFAS profile and co‑contaminants may not represent other leachates.
Short‑chain PFAS behavior is characterized only by removal percentages; detailed mass balance, aerosol losses, and by‑products in off‑gas are not fully quantified.
Energy demand is discussed qualitatively as cost‑ and energy‑efficient; no full energy audit or cost breakdown is presented.
sources.title: Pilot-Scale Continuous Foam Fractionation for the Removal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from Landfill Leachate

sources.citation: McCleaf P, Stefansson W, Ahrens L. Water Research. 2023;232:119688.

evidence_chunks.text: "The present work examined a novel PFAS removal scheme for drinking water using NF filtration with treatment of the resulting NF concentrate via foam fractionation (FF) with and without co‑surfactants."
"The NF-pilot removed 98% of PFAS from AFFF contaminated groundwater producing permeate with 1.4 ng L−1 total PFAS."
Using foam fractionation on the NF concentrate resulted in a total PFAS removal efficiency of 90%, which improved to 94% with addition of a cationic co‑surfactant.
"The resulting foamate composed approximately 2% of the NF feedwater volume and contained greater than 3000 ng L−1 PFAS or 41 times greater than the NF feedwater."

Addition of the cationic co‑surfactant increased removal of shorter‑chain PFAS in the concentrate FF step, with reported increases of 37% for PFPeA, 9% for PFHxA, and 34% for PFBS, leading to 59%, 99% and 96% overall removal efficiencies respectively.

source_limitations: Treatment train is specific to AFFF‑impacted groundwater and a particular NF membrane; generalization to other feed waters or membranes is uncertain.
Short‑chain PFAS results are limited to a subset of analytes (e.g., PFPeA, PFHxA, PFBS).
Energy demand and life‑cycle impacts of combined NF+FF are not quantified beyond qualitative discussion.
sources.title: Drinking water nanofiltration with concentrate foam fractionation—A novel approach for removal of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

sources.citation: Vo PHN, Nguyen TTP, Nguyen HTM, et al. Water Research. 2024;253:121300.

evidence_chunks.text: "This study aims to (i) assess the effectiveness of the ozone foam fractionation system to remove PFAS from landfill leachate, and (ii) quantify equilibrium PFAS adsorption onto the gas-water interface of ozone bubbles, followed by a comparison with air foam fractionation."
"The results show that ozone foam fractionation is effective for PFAS removal from landfill leachate, with more than 90% long-chain PFAS removed."

The optimized operating conditions included an ozone gas flow rate of about 1 L/min, ozone dose around 43 mg/L, and minimizing foamate production to roughly 4% wettability to reduce residual volume while maintaining high PFAS removal.

Equilibrium modeling indicated that the surface excess of PFAS on air bubbles was 20–40% higher than on ozone bubbles at the same concentration, but overall PFAS removal by ozone foam fractionation from landfill leachate remained substantial.

source_limitations: Study is based on one landfill leachate; behavior in other matrices (e.g., groundwater, municipal wastewater) is not demonstrated.
Focus is on long‑chain PFAS; short‑chain removal performance and enrichment factors are less detailed.
Downstream treatment or disposal of ozonated foamate is not experimentally evaluated; only the concentration step is characterized.
Energy consumption of ozone generation and overall process is not fully quantified.
sources.title: PFAS removal from landfill leachate by ozone foam fractionation: System optimization and adsorption quantification

sources.citation: Wang Y, Ji Y, Tishchenko V, Huang Q. Chemosphere. 2022;311:137004.

evidence_chunks.text: "This work presented a systematic study on PFAS removal by foam fractionation (FF). Experiments were conducted on both laboratory-spiked and environmental water samples containing PFASs."
The abstract reports that higher air flow, greater ionic strength, and addition of thickener increased PFAS removal in the defoamed bottom solutions and intensified enrichment in the collected foam.

Foam fractionation treatments of a landfill leachate, groundwater contaminated by aqueous film‑forming foams, and a wastewater treatment plant effluent were evaluated, with removals above about 70% for most monitored PFAS except the shortest alkyl chains.
"PFAS concentrations in the final collected foams were up to over 30 × than that in the original samples."

The authors conclude that foam fractionation can produce low‑volume, highly concentrated PFAS solutions from a range of environmental waters, illustrating its function as a concentration step prior to further treatment.

source_limitations: Only the abstract was accessible; detailed experimental conditions, PFAS speciation, and operating durations are not available from the inspected record.
Short‑chain PFAS behavior is summarized qualitatively as lower removal; specific chain‑length‑dependent data and mass balances are not visible.
Energy consumption, foamate management, and downstream destruction methods are not discussed in the abstract.
sources.title: Removing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in water by foam fractionation

sources.citation: Burns D, Murphy P, Hinrichsen H. Conference poster, Chlorinated Conference 2022.

evidence_chunks.text: "A three year (2021-2024) commercial scale field trial (330 m3/day) to assess the viability of the Surface Active Foam Fractionation (SAFF®) process to remove PFAS compounds from landfill…"

"The EPOC Enviro SAFF40 has demonstrated, at commercial-scale (330 m3/day) remediation of PFAS-contaminated landfill leachate, with final treatment results of, ≤2.34 ng/l PFOS, ≤1.28 ng/l PFOA, and ≤1.00 ng/l PFHxS, which corresponds to removal percentages of ≥98.7% PFOS, ≥99.7% PFOA, and ≥98.8% PFHxS."
"During this period approximately 80,000 m3 of leachate was successfully treated. The trial was completed with no exceedances of criteria compounds and without the need for complex pre-treatment."

The poster notes that removal percentages for PFAS species increase monotonically with the gas–liquid adsorption coefficient and that short‑chain species such as PFHxA, PFBS, PFPeA and PFBA are less amenable to removal, limiting summed PFAS removal to about 55% when these non‑criterion short chains are included.

"The end product of the three fractionation stages is a highly concentrated liquid waste which is amenable to on-site destruction utilizing a range of commercially available fluorocarbon destruction technologies (e.g., supercritical water oxidation, plasma, electrochemical oxidation or reductive defluorination) or off-site destruction at a high temperature thermal incineration plant."

source_limitations: Conference poster with limited methodological detail and no full peer‑reviewed article is provided.
Foamate composition, volume reduction factors, and long‑term operational stability data are summarized but not presented as full time series.
Energy consumption, detailed cost analysis, and specific destruction technology performance for the concentrated waste are not reported.
sources.title: PFAS landfill leachate case study: Surface Active Foam Fractionation (SAFF®) Sweden (Tveta landfill)

sources.citation: Envytech. SAFF – Surface Active Foam Fractionation technology poster (Arlanda Airport surface runoff and Tveta landfill leachate case studies).

evidence_chunks.text: "Envytech offers the SAFF - Surface Active Foam Fractionation technology… SAFF does not use filter materials, only air and electricity, and is completely unaffected by other pollutants such as metals or organic substances, particles, pH, nutrients or other water chemistry."

The poster describes a multi‑stage SAFF system in which the second fractionation step produces a drier foam that is removed by vacuum, increasing PFAS concentration by up to about 1,500 times so that the total concentration increase after two stages is roughly 10,000‑fold.

A table summarizing PFAS concentrations for untreated water, treated water and treated water with detergent at a PFAS‑impacted site indicates high removals for long‑chain species (e.g., 100% PFOS, PFOA, 6:2 FTS, PFDA, PFNA; 97–99% PFHxS) and more modest removals for short‑chain PFAS such as PFHxA, PFPeA, PFBA and PFBS (0–62%).

For the Tveta landfill leachate, the poster notes that leachate contains nitrogen, phosphorus, DOC, TOC, suspended solids, larvae, and algae, and that previous treatment trials with various filter technologies had failed, whereas full‑scale SAFF treatment is being carried out to meet a discharge limit of 50 ng/L PFOS to the receiving wastewater treatment plant.

source_limitations: Conference poster format limits the description of experimental design, sampling frequency, and analytical methods.
Foamate volumes, precise enrichment factors for each stage, and long‑term operational data are only qualitatively indicated.
Energy consumption and detailed economic analysis of multi‑stage SAFF treatment and downstream destruction options are not quantified.
sources.title: SAFF – Surface Active Foam Fractionation technology (multi-site performance poster)

sources.citation: Newman P. ESAA Remediation Technologies Symposium abstract. 2026.

evidence_chunks.text: "ECT2 designed a combined system of foam fractionation on the landfill leachate to remove PFAS and Superloading adsorptive media treatment on the concentrated liquid waste (foamate), thereby converting the foam fractionate liquid to a solid waste."

The system progressed from pilot to full‑scale, with 1.5 years of full‑scale operational data by the end of 2025, and operates with lead‑lag Foam X‑3000 foam fractionators that treat approximately 100 gallons per minute of landfill leachate.
Treatment goals include removal of 75% of PFAS mass, with less than about 45% of the PFAS mass comprised of short‑chain compounds.

"The resulting foamate is treated in successive adsorptive media beds and then re-blended into the foam fractionation system influent. The adsorptive media is then returned with sequestered PFAS to the landfill, which is a simple waste management strategy that can be employed at similar facilities."

The abstract reports that the foamate Superloading process yielded up to an additional 500‑fold concentration of waste into a solid media format, and overall a waste concentration factor of approximately 1000–2000‑fold for the landfill, while maintaining stable foam fractionation performance through long‑term chemical dosing strategies.

source_limitations: Document is a one‑page conference abstract; detailed operational data, PFAS speciation, and analytical results are not shown.
Short‑chain PFAS behavior is reported only via an overall mass fraction target; individual short‑chain species removals are not provided.
Energy demand, media replacement frequency, and destruction or long‑term stability of the PFAS‑loaded solid media are not addressed.
sources.title: Converting PFAS-Impacted Landfill Leachate Waste from a Liquid to a Solid: Using Full-Scale Foam Fractionation and Media Superloading to Minimize Waste and Reduce Risk

sources.citation: [Authors not fully listed in excerpt]. Frontiers in Environmental Science. 2026;14:1771570.

evidence_chunks.text: "Foam fractionation is emerging as a promising option to remove and concentrate PFAS from polluted water and soil resources. Here, we investigate the electrochemical treatment of foamate resulting from the simultaneous application of soil washing and foam fractionation for the remediation of PFAS-contaminated soil."

The study evaluates boron‑doped diamond (BDD) electrochemical oxidation of PFAS‑enriched foamate and examines the effects of applied current density, flow rate, initial PFAS concentration and organic matter content on treatment performance.

The authors note that combined soil washing and foam fractionation generate a concentrated foam stream, and that additional treatment is required to degrade the PFAS load; electrochemical oxidation is proposed and tested as this downstream step.

The article emphasizes that process parameters such as current density and recirculation (mass transfer) strongly influence the efficiency of PFAS degradation in fractionated foam, and that boron‑doped diamond electrodes showed very good performance for PFAS‑contaminated solutions.

source_limitations: The work focuses on treatment of foamate generated from soil washing and foam fractionation, not directly on the foam fractionation step itself.
Results are specific to boron‑doped diamond electrodes and lab‑scale conditions; scalability to field systems and other electrode materials is not assessed.
The composition of the incoming foamate stream (including short‑ vs long‑chain PFAS and co‑contaminants) is not fully detailed in the excerpted sections.
sources.title: Electrochemical treatment of PFAS in fractionated foam

evidence_chunks.text: The paper reports on the use of foam fractionation to generate PFAS-enriched foamate and then evaluates electrochemical oxidation via boron-doped diamond electrodes to remove PFAS from the foamate under stirred batch conditions (~200 mL).

The authors conducted experiments with radiolabeled PFOA (14C‑PFOA) spiked into distilled and field‑collected water to follow the distribution and fate of PFAS between bulk water, foam, and during electrochemical treatment.

evidence_chunks.section: Conclusions (from search snippet and cited review)
evidence_chunks.text: The study demonstrates proof‑of‑concept that foam fractionation followed by electrochemical oxidation can be used in tandem to treat PFAS‑contaminated water, with long‑chain PFAS degraded more efficiently than short‑chain PFAS.

source_limitations: Full HTML/PDF content could not be accessed directly due to rate limiting; evidence relies on the abstract text visible in the inspected search representation and secondary review citations.
Quantitative removal percentages, enrichment factors, and energy consumption of the combined FF–EO treatment are not explicitly available.
Experiments are bench‑scale in small volumes; transferability to pilot or full‑scale systems is uncertain.
sources.title: Remediating Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)-Contaminated Water by Foam Fractionation and Electrochemical Oxidation
